questions.q: Which keyword is used to define a class in Python?
questions.explain: A class definition starts with the keyword class, then the class name and a colon, e.g. class Dog:. Everything indented under that line is the class body.
why_wrong: def defines a function or method, not a class
object is the built-in base class that every class inherits from, not a keyword for defining one
struct is a C/C++ keyword; Python has no struct statement

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.explain: Dog("Tommy") runs __init__, which stores "Tommy" in the instance attribute self.name. d.name reads that attribute, and print() shows a string's contents without quotes.
why_wrong: print() shows a string without its quotes; quotes appear only in the repr form, e.g. inside a printed list
d.name gives the attribute's value, not the attribute's name
The class name is not printed; d.name is the string stored inside the object

questions.q: Which special method does Python call automatically when a new object is created, so that it can set up the object's attributes?
questions.explain: __init__ is the constructor: writing Dog("Tommy") creates the object and immediately runs __init__ with self bound to the new object and the other arguments passed in. Instance attributes such as self.name are normally created there.
why_wrong: __str__ is called by print() and str() to get a text form, not when the object is created
__del__ is the destructor, called when the object is about to be destroyed
__eq__ is called by the == operator to compare two objects

questions.q: In object-oriented terminology, what is an individual object created from a class called?
questions.explain: A class is a blueprint, and each object built from it, e.g. d = Dog("Tommy"), is an instance of that class. Creating it is called instantiation, and isinstance(d, Dog) is True.
why_wrong: A method is a function defined inside the class, not an object made from it
An attribute is a named value stored on a class or object, such as d.name
A subclass is another class that inherits from it, not an object created from it

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.code:
class Student:
    school = "LPU"

s = Student()
print(s.school)
questions.explain: school is a class attribute: it is defined in the class body and shared by every instance. s has no instance attribute called school, so s.school falls back to the class and finds "LPU", which print() shows without quotes.
why_wrong: print() shows a string without its quotes
No error: when an instance lacks an attribute, Python looks it up on the class next
The attribute exists with the value "LPU"; nothing assigns None to it

questions.q: In the class below, which one is an instance attribute?
questions.explain: An instance attribute belongs to one particular object and is normally created by assigning to self.something inside __init__, so every Car can have its own colour. wheels is assigned in the class body, which makes it a class attribute shared by all Car objects.
why_wrong: wheels is assigned in the class body, so it is a class attribute shared by all instances
Car is the name of the class itself, not an attribute
__init__ is a method (the constructor), not a data attribute

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.explain: Box(3, 4) runs __init__ with self = the new object, w = 3 and h = 4, so it stores b.w = 3 and b.h = 4. Then b.w * b.h = 3 × 4 = 12.
why_wrong: Adds w + h instead of multiplying w * h
Box(3, 4) is a correct call: self is passed automatically, so the two arguments go to w and h
Both attributes exist because __init__ creates self.w and self.h

questions.q: Which line correctly defines a class B that inherits from class A?
questions.explain: In Python the parent class is written in parentheses after the child's name: class B(A):. B then gets every attribute and method of A that it does not redefine itself.
why_wrong: extends is Java syntax; in Python this line is a SyntaxError
This makes A the child of B, which is the reverse relationship
inherits is not a Python keyword; this line is a SyntaxError

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.explain: Cat defines its own sound(), which overrides Animal.sound(). For a Cat object Python finds sound in Cat first, so the child's version runs and the parent's version is never called.
why_wrong: The parent's method would run only if Cat did not define its own sound()
An overriding method replaces the parent's; Python does not run both and join the results
Cat.sound() returns "Meow", so there is a value to print

questions.q: What is it called when a child class defines a method with the same name as a method in its parent class, so that the child's version is used for child objects?
questions.explain: Overriding happens between a parent and a child: the child redefines an inherited method, and calls on a child object use the child's version. The parent's version can still be reached from the child with super().
why_wrong: Overloading means one method name accepting different argument lists, not a child replacing a parent's method
Encapsulation is bundling data with the methods that work on it and restricting direct access
Instantiation is creating an object from a class

questions.q: Inside a class, which attribute name makes Python apply name mangling (data hiding)?
questions.explain: A name that starts with two underscores (and does not also end with two) is name-mangled: inside class Account, self.__balance is stored as _Account__balance. A single leading underscore is only a convention meaning 'internal, please don't touch'.
why_wrong: One leading underscore is only a naming convention; Python does not mangle it
A plain name is fully public, with no hiding at all
Trailing underscores do not trigger mangling; only two leading underscores do

questions.q: What happens when the code below runs?
questions.explain: Inside the class, self.__pin is name-mangled and stored as _Account__pin. Outside the class, a.__pin is looked up literally, no attribute with that exact name exists, so Python raises AttributeError.
why_wrong: The value is stored as _Account__pin, so the plain name __pin is not found from outside the class
A missing attribute raises an error; Python never quietly returns None for it
The code is valid syntax; the error happens only when the print line runs

questions.q: A Python class defines two methods with the same name but different numbers of parameters. Which method does the class keep?
options: Both; Python picks one by the number of arguments
Neither; defining the same name twice is a SyntaxError
questions.explain: A def statement simply binds a name, so the second def with the same name rebinds it and the first method is lost. Python has no Java-style overloading by parameter count; default arguments or *args are used to get a similar effect.
why_wrong: The later def rebinds the name and overwrites the first one
That is overloading as in Java or C++; Python does not choose a method by argument count
Redefining a name is legal; no SyntaxError is raised

questions.q: Which special method must a class define so that the + operator works between two of its objects?
questions.explain: Python turns a + b into a.__add__(b). Defining __add__ in a class overloads the + operator for its objects, which is called operator overloading.
why_wrong: __init__ runs when an object is created, not when + is used
__str__ controls the text that print() shows, not the + operator
__len__ is called by len(), not by +

questions.q: What happens when the code below runs?
questions.explain: g.hello() really means Greeter.hello(g): Python always passes the object as the first argument. hello was written with no parameters, so it cannot accept that argument and Python raises TypeError (takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given).
why_wrong: The method body never runs; the call fails because g is passed in and hello() has no parameter to receive it
hello exists on the class, so the lookup succeeds; the failure is the argument count
No undefined name is used; the problem is the missing self parameter

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.explain: P defines no __eq__, so a == b falls back to comparing identity: a and b are two separate objects, giving False. a.x == b.x compares the ints 1 and 1, giving True.
why_wrong: Equal attribute values do not make two objects equal unless the class defines __eq__
a.x and b.x are both the int 1, so the second comparison is True
Swaps the two results: the object comparison is the one that gives False

questions.q: Which statement about self is NOT true?
options: Python passes the object automatically as the first argument when you call obj.method()
Inside a method, self.name refers to the name attribute of the object the method was called on
self is a reserved keyword, so naming the first parameter this instead causes a SyntaxError
A method defined with no parameters at all raises TypeError when called as obj.method()
questions.explain: self is only a naming convention: Python passes the object to the first parameter whatever it is called, so def show(this): works. Everyone uses self for readability, but it is not a keyword. Leaving the first parameter out completely is what causes the error.
why_wrong: This is true: obj.method() is equivalent to Class.method(obj)
This is true: self is the calling object, so self.name is that object's attribute
This is true: the object is still passed, and a method with no parameters cannot accept it

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.code:
class Team:
    size = 5

a = Team()
b = Team()
a.size = 8
print(a.size, b.size, Team.size)
questions.explain: a.size = 8 does not change the class attribute; it creates a new instance attribute on a only. b has no instance attribute, so b.size falls back to Team.size, which is still 5.
why_wrong: Assigning through an instance does not update the shared class attribute, so b and Team keep 5
Assigning through a creates an attribute on a; it does not write to the class
b has no size of its own and reads Team.size, which is still 5, so it cannot see a's 8

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.code:
class Bag:
    items = []
    def add(self, x):
        self.items.append(x)

p, q = Bag(), Bag()
p.add(1)
q.add(2)
print(p.items)
questions.explain: items = [] sits in the class body, so there is one list shared by every Bag object. self.items.append(x) never assigns to self.items; it finds the class list and mutates it, so p.add(1) and q.add(2) both add to the same list.
why_wrong: Would be right only if each object had its own list; q.add(2) appends to the same shared list
The 1 from p.add(1) is still there; q's append adds to the list, it does not replace it
append changes the shared list in place, so it is no longer empty

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.explain: isinstance(v, Vehicle) follows inheritance: Bike is a subclass of Vehicle, so it is True. type(v) returns the exact class Bike, and Bike == Vehicle is False.
why_wrong: type() reports the exact class Bike and ignores the parent, so the second value is False
isinstance() accepts subclasses, so a Bike object counts as a Vehicle
Both are reversed: isinstance follows inheritance, type does not

questions.q: What happens when the code below runs?
questions.explain: Student defines its own __init__, which overrides Person.__init__ and never calls it through super().__init__(). So self.name = "Asha" never runs, s only has roll, and reading s.name raises AttributeError.
why_wrong: The parent's __init__ does not run automatically once the child defines its own __init__
A missing attribute raises an error; it is not silently None
Student() is called with the right number of arguments; the error comes from the missing attribute

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.explain: For class W(Y, Z), Python searches W first and then the parents from left to right: W, Y, Z, object. W has no who(), Y does, so Y.who runs and Y is printed.
why_wrong: Z is searched only after Y, so its who() would be used only if Y had none
Only the first method found runs; Python does not call both parents' versions
Two parents having a method with the same name is legal; the search order settles which one runs

questions.q: After the code below runs, which expression raises AttributeError?
questions.explain: Inside the class, self.__x is mangled to _Priv__x, and get_x() uses the same mangled name, so it returns 10. Outside the class, p.__x is not mangled, no attribute with that exact name exists, and it raises AttributeError.
why_wrong: A single underscore is only a convention, so p._y simply returns 20
This is the mangled name the value is actually stored under, so it returns 10
Code inside the class writes self.__x, which is mangled the same way, so it returns 10

questions.q: Which statement about data hiding in Python is NOT true?
options: A single leading underscore, as in self._y, makes Python block access to it from outside the class
Inside class Priv, self.__x is actually stored under the name _Priv__x
Name mangling is not strict access control; p._Priv__x still reaches the value
Methods of the class itself can read self.__x normally
questions.explain: A single leading underscore is only a convention meaning 'internal, please don't use'; Python does not mangle it, and obj._y works from anywhere. Only two leading underscores trigger name mangling, and even that can be bypassed through the mangled name.
why_wrong: This is true: two leading underscores inside class Priv are renamed to _Priv__x
This is true: mangling only renames the attribute, so the mangled name still works from outside
This is true: code inside the class is mangled the same way, so self.__x works there

questions.q: What happens when the code below runs?
questions.explain: The second def add rebinds the name, so only add(self, a, b, c) survives. c.add(1, 2) supplies a and b but not c, so Python raises TypeError: missing 1 required positional argument: 'c'.
why_wrong: The two-parameter add was overwritten by the second definition, so Python cannot choose it
6 would need a third argument, but only 1 and 2 are passed
Defining the same method name twice is legal syntax; the error comes only from the call

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.explain: V(2) + V(3) calls V(2).__add__(V(3)), which returns V(2 + 3), a new V object with x = 5. So s is a V object and s.x is 5.
why_wrong: + works here because V defines __add__; without it, this would be the TypeError
__add__ returns a V object, which has an x attribute, not a bare int
self.x and other.x are the ints 2 and 3, so + adds them; it does not join them as text

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.code:
class Box:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
a = Box(1)
b = a
c = Box(1)
b.v = 5
print(a.v, c.v, a is b, a == c)
questions.explain: b = a does not copy the object. It makes b a second name for the same Box, so b.v = 5 also changes a.v, and a is b is True. c is a separate Box whose v stays 1. Box defines no __eq__, so a == c falls back to identity and is False even though both started with v = 1.
why_wrong: Treats b = a as making a copy. It only binds a second name to the same object, so changing b.v changes a.v.
Assumes == compares attribute values. Without an __eq__ method, == checks identity, and a and c are different objects.
Makes both mistakes: it treats b = a as a separate copy (so a is b would be False) and assumes == compares the stored values.

questions.q: What does the code below print, or which exception does it raise?
questions.explain: Inside __init__, side = s creates only a local variable, and it disappears when __init__ returns. To create an attribute you must write self.side = s. When area() reads self.side, Python looks for an attribute named side on the object, finds none, and raises AttributeError: 'Square' object has no attribute 'side'.
why_wrong: Assumes every variable assigned inside __init__ becomes an attribute. Without self. it is just a local variable.
NameError is for a bare name that cannot be found. self.side is an attribute lookup on an object, and a failed attribute lookup raises AttributeError.
Python never gives None for a missing attribute. Reading an attribute that was never created raises an error.

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.code:
class Ticket:
    issued = 0
    def __init__(self):
        Ticket.issued += 1
        self.no = Ticket.issued
t1, t2, t3 = Ticket(), Ticket(), Ticket()
print(t1.no, t3.no, t1.issued)
questions.explain: issued is a class attribute, and Ticket.issued += 1 updates that one shared counter, so it becomes 1, 2 and then 3 as the three objects are made. self.no = Ticket.issued copies the current number into each object's own attribute, so t1.no is 1 and t3.no is 3. t1 has no instance attribute called issued, so t1.issued reads the class value, which is now 3.
why_wrong: Assumes t1.issued was frozen when t1 was created. t1 has no issued of its own, so it reads the shared class value, which is now 3.
Assumes self.no stays linked to Ticket.issued. The assignment stored the number 1 in t1.no, and later changes to the counter do not affect it.
Assumes each object gets its own fresh copy of issued starting at 0. Ticket.issued += 1 updates the single counter shared by the whole class.

questions.q: What does the code below print, or which exception does it raise?
questions.code:
class Car:
    wheels = 4
a = Car()
b = Car()
a.wheels = 3
Car.wheels = 6
print(a.wheels, b.wheels, Car.wheels)
questions.explain: a.wheels = 3 creates an instance attribute on a only. It shadows the class attribute for a and leaves b alone. Car.wheels = 6 then changes the class attribute. b has no wheels of its own, so it reads the class value 6, while a still finds its own 3 first.
why_wrong: Assumes b copied the value 4 when it was created. b has no wheels of its own and reads the class attribute each time, and that is now 6.
Assumes changing Car.wheels overrides every object. a has its own wheels = 3, and Python finds that before the class attribute.
Assumes a class attribute cannot be assigned through an instance. Python allows it: a.wheels = 3 simply creates a new attribute on a.

questions.q: A results program has a Student class whose body contains the class attribute pass_mark = 40, and several Student objects (s1, s2, …) already exist. None of them has its own pass_mark attribute. The university now raises the pass mark to 45 for every student. Which single statement, written at the top level of the program, does this?
questions.explain: Assigning through the class name rebinds the class attribute itself. Every object without its own pass_mark reads the class value, so Student.pass_mark = 45 reaches all existing and future Student objects. Assigning through one object would instead create a new instance attribute on that object alone.
why_wrong: Assigning through an object creates a new instance attribute on s1 only. s2 and the others still read the class value 40.
self exists only as a method's parameter, so at the top level it is undefined (NameError). Even inside a method it would change only one object.
At the top level this creates an ordinary global variable with no connection to the Student class.

questions.q: What happens when the code below runs?
options: It raises TypeError, because super().__init__() must be the first statement in __init__
It raises AttributeError, because a Dog object does not receive the name attribute from Animal
questions.explain: The statements in __init__ run in order. Dog's __init__ first sets self.sound = 'woof', then super().__init__(name) runs Animal's __init__ on the same object. That sets self.name = 'Rex' and overwrites self.sound with 'silent'. Python does not require the super() call to come first, so the output is Rex silent.
why_wrong: Assumes the child's value always wins. The parent's __init__ runs after 'woof' was stored and overwrites sound with 'silent'.
Python has no rule about where the super().__init__() call goes. It can appear anywhere in __init__ and simply runs at that point.
super().__init__(name) does run Animal's __init__, and that creates self.name on the Dog object.

questions.q: A bank charges a ₹10 fee on every withdrawal from a Savings account, so the developer overrides withdraw() as shown in the code below. What does it print?
questions.explain: s.withdraw(20) finds Savings.withdraw first, because the child's override wins. That method calls Account.withdraw(self, 30) and passes the same object s explicitly, so the parent's code runs on s and subtracts 30. s.bal = 100 − 30 = 70.
why_wrong: Assumes the parent's withdraw runs instead of the override. Savings.withdraw is found first and adds the ₹10 fee.
Assumes both versions run separately (20 and then 30). The parent's code runs only once, when the override calls it with 30.
Assumes Account.withdraw(self, ...) changes the class rather than the object. Passing self makes it work on s and reduce s.bal.

questions.q: A smart thermostat must accept only settings from 10 to 30 degrees, so its temperature is hidden and can be changed only through set_temp(), which returns the current setting. What does the code below print?
questions.explain: set_temp(25) passes the 10 <= t <= 30 check and stores 25 in the hidden attribute. set_temp(45) fails the check, so nothing is stored, and the method returns the current value, 25. The class's own methods can use self.__temp freely, because name mangling only hides the name from code outside the class.
why_wrong: Ignores the range check. 45 fails 10 <= t <= 30, so the assignment is skipped.
Forgets that the first call already stored 25. A rejected value leaves the last accepted value in place, not the starting 20.
Assumes __temp is hidden from the class's own methods too. Inside the class, self.__temp works normally.

questions.q: What happens when the code below runs?
options: It prints [7], then print(r.__fmt(7)) raises AttributeError
It prints [7] twice, because name mangling hides attributes but not methods
print(r.show(7)) raises AttributeError, because a hidden method cannot be called even from inside its class
It prints [7], then print(r.__fmt(7)) raises NameError
questions.explain: Name mangling applies to method names too: inside the class, __fmt is stored as _Report__fmt. show() is written inside the class, so self.__fmt(x) is translated to self._Report__fmt(x), which works and prints [7]. The last line is outside the class, so r.__fmt is not translated, no attribute with that name exists, and Python raises AttributeError.
why_wrong: Mangling applies to any name with two leading underscores defined in a class, and that includes methods.
Inside the class, self.__fmt is translated to the mangled name, so the class's own methods can call a hidden method.
r.__fmt is an attribute lookup on an object, so the failure is AttributeError. NameError is for bare variable names.

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.explain: The in operator compares items with ==, and Point overloads == through __eq__ to compare x values. The new Point(2) has the same x as pts[1], so Point(2) in pts is True. is checks identity, and the new Point(2) is a different object from pts[1], so that is False.
why_wrong: Assumes in looks for the same object. in uses ==, and __eq__ has overloaded == to compare x values.
Assumes objects that compare equal are the same object. is checks identity, and the new Point(2) is a separate object.
Assumes in only works with built-in values such as numbers and strings. It works with any object and uses that object's __eq__.

questions.q: A geometry class needs one method area that works both as sq.area(5) for a square and as sq.area(4, 6) for a rectangle, where sq is an object of the class. Python keeps only the last definition of a method name, so the class cannot hold two versions. Which method header lets both calls work?
questions.explain: Python has no overloading by number of parameters, and the usual substitute is a default argument. With def area(self, a, b=None):, sq.area(5) sets a = 5 and leaves b as None, while sq.area(4, 6) sets a = 4 and b = 6. The body then checks whether b is None, and sq fills self automatically in both calls.
why_wrong: b has no default, so sq.area(5) raises TypeError for the missing argument b.
A parameter without a default cannot follow one that has a default, so this header is a SyntaxError.
Forgets self: sq goes into a, so sq.area(5) puts 5 into b and sq.area(4, 6) passes too many arguments (TypeError).

questions.q: What does the code below print, or which exception does it raise?
questions.explain: Square's area(self, scale) completely overrides Shape's area, even though the parameters differ. Python does not keep both versions and choose one by argument count. Square(3).area() therefore calls Square.area with no value for scale and raises TypeError: missing 1 required positional argument: 'scale'.
why_wrong: Assumes Python picks the parent's zero-argument area() because it matches the call. The child's method replaces it, whatever its parameters.
Assumes the missing scale is simply skipped. A required parameter with no value is an error.
The method is found (Square.area). The failure is in the call's arguments, and that is a TypeError.

questions.q: What does the code below print, or which exception does it raise?
questions.explain: Inside quad, Python looks up the bare name double as a local and then a global variable, not as a method of the class. No such variable exists, so Python raises NameError: name 'double' is not defined. The correct call is self.double(x), which would make quad(3) return 6 · 2 = 12.
why_wrong: Assumes methods of the same class can call each other by bare name, as in Java or C++. Python needs self.double(x).
Assumes double receives too few arguments. The name is never found, so no call happens and the error is NameError.
AttributeError comes from obj.name lookups. A bare name like double is searched in local and global scope, so the failure is NameError.

questions.q: In the code below, hello() was written without self. Which of these calls runs without raising an error?
questions.explain: Calling a method through an object passes that object automatically as the first argument. g.hello() and Greeter().hello() therefore call hello with 1 argument, but hello takes 0, so both raise TypeError. Calling through the class, Greeter.hello(), passes nothing automatically, so hello gets 0 arguments and returns 'hi'. Greeter.hello(g) passes the object by hand, exactly as g.hello() does, so it fails too.
why_wrong: Python passes g automatically as the first argument, but hello() accepts none, so this raises TypeError.
Passing g by hand is exactly what g.hello() does behind the scenes, so hello() again receives 1 argument and raises TypeError.
A newly created object is still an instance, so Python passes it automatically and hello() raises TypeError.

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.code:
class Bag:
    items = []
    def add(self, x):
        self.items = self.items + [x]
a = Bag()
b = Bag()
a.add(1)
b.add(2)
print(a.items, b.items, Bag.items)
questions.explain: self.items + [x] builds a brand-new list, and assigning it to self.items creates an instance attribute on that one object. So a gets its own [1] and b its own [2]. The class list is only read, never changed, so Bag.items stays []. If the method had used self.items.append(x), it would have mutated the shared class list and all three would print [1, 2].
why_wrong: Treats self.items = self.items + [x] like self.items.append(x). + builds a new list and the assignment attaches it to one object, so the shared list is never mutated.
Correctly gives each object its own list but assumes the class list also collects every item. + only reads the class list and never changes it.
Assumes an assignment through self inside a method is lost when the method ends. self.items = ... stores a real attribute on the object.

questions.q: What does the code below print, or which exception does it raise?
questions.explain: A method is just an attribute of the class, and attribute lookup checks the object's own attributes before the class. __init__ gave s an instance attribute area = 10, so s.area is the integer 10, which hides the method. s.area() then tries to call 10 and raises TypeError: 'int' object is not callable.
why_wrong: Assumes methods take priority. The instance attribute area = 10 is found first and hides the method defined in the class.
Correctly finds that s.area is 10 but ignores the (): Python cannot call an integer.
The attribute exists (it is the integer 10). The failure is in calling it, and that is a TypeError.

questions.q: What does the code below print, or which exception does it raise?
questions.explain: C().f() runs C's own f, which returns 'C' + super().f(). super() searches the parents in order: B has no f, so the search continues to A, and A.f runs with self still being the C object. Inside it, Python looks up self.g() starting from C, and B's g is found first, returning 'b'. So the result is 'C' + 'A' + 'b' = CAb.
why_wrong: Assumes self.g() inside A.f calls A's own g. self is a C object, so the lookup starts at C and finds B's g first.
Ignores C's own f. C().f() runs C's f first, and that adds 'C' before calling the parent version.
Assumes super() searches only the immediate parent B, which has no f. The search continues up the chain and finds A.f.

questions.q: What does the code below print?
questions.explain: For class W(Y, Z), Python searches W, then Y, then Z, and only then the shared base X. The order is left to right, and a common base comes after all of its children. Y has no hi of its own, so the search reaches Z and W().hi() returns 'Z'. Y's own search order is just Y, X, so Y().hi() returns 'X'.
why_wrong: Searches depth-first (W, Y, then Y's parent X) before reaching Z. Python puts the common base X after both Y and Z.
Assumes defining W links Y to its sibling Z. A Y object searches only Y and X, so it still gets X's hi.
Assumes Python forbids a class whose two parents share a base. Multiple inheritance is allowed, and this search order resolves it.

questions.q: What does the code below print, or which exception does it raise?
questions.explain: Name mangling uses the name of the class in which the code is written. In Parent, self.__code becomes self._Parent__code. In Child, self.__code is translated to self._Child__code, which was never created, so reveal() raises AttributeError: 'Child' object has no attribute '_Child__code'.

The failing lookup is an attribute on self, and that raises AttributeError. NameError is for bare variable names.

questions.q: A student tries to get around data hiding by setting the hidden balance to 0 from outside the class, as in the code below. What does it print?
questions.explain: Inside the class, self.__bal is stored as _Account__bal = 500. The line acc.__bal = 0 is outside the class, so Python does not mangle it. It creates a separate new attribute literally named __bal. get() reads _Account__bal (500), and acc.__bal outside the class reads the new attribute (0).
why_wrong: Assumes the outside assignment overwrote the hidden balance. It created a different attribute, so get() still returns 500.
Assumes acc.__bal outside the class reads the hidden value. It reads the new attribute that was just set to 0.
Python does not block the assignment. acc.__bal = 0 simply creates a new attribute, and after that acc.__bal can be read.

why_wrong: Assumes + always produces a new object and leaves a unchanged. This __add__ modifies self (which is a) and returns it.
Sees that a changed but assumes c is a separate object. __add__ returns self, so c and a are one object.
Assumes __add__ must build and return a new object. Any value may be returned, and returning self is legal.

questions.q: What happens when the code below runs?
options: It raises TypeError at the line y = 3 * m
It raises TypeError at the line x = m * 3, because __mul__ expects another Money object
y becomes the int 150, so the print line raises AttributeError
questions.explain: An expression a * b calls the __mul__ of the LEFT operand. m * 3 calls Money.__mul__(m, 3) and gives Money(150). 3 * m asks int to multiply itself by a Money object, which int does not support. Money defines no reversed version (__rmul__), so Python raises TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for *: 'int' and 'Money'.
why_wrong: Assumes defining __mul__ makes * work in both orders. It only handles a Money object on the left.
This __mul__ multiplies self.amt by k directly, so any number works as k, and m * 3 gives Money(150).
int cannot multiply a Money object, so Python raises TypeError at y = 3 * m and never reaches the print line.
